This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) examines PM2.5 exposure (total mass and constituents), (3) includes respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome, (4) uses time-series analysis design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 3.47% increase with 95% CI: 2.03, 4.94% for respiratory admissions), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include respiratory hospitalizations among 214 disease groups studied, (4) time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for hospital admissions per µg/m3 increase in PM2.5, and (6) published in English. While the study examines multiple disease outcomes, respiratory diseases are explicitly mentioned as one of the outcomes with positive associations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) examines PM2.5 exposure (among other particulate matter sizes), (3) outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (percent increase in risk with 95% confidence intervals implied), and (6) published in English. The study explicitly states PM2.5 exposure was associated with 2.2% increase in respiratory admissions per 10μg/m3 increase.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations, (4) study design is explicitly time-series analysis, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with credible intervals (e.g., 0.75% increase per 10 μg/m3 with 95% CI), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines circulatory hospitalizations, respiratory hospitalizations are a primary outcome with specific effect estimates reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as one of the exposures, (3) respiratory ED visits are analyzed as outcomes (asthma, COPD, respiratory infections), (4) time-series study design, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported (e.g., 7.6% increase in asthma visits per 8.2 µg/m3 PM2.5, 95% CI 5.1-10.1), and (6) published in English. Although the study examines multiple pollutants and both cardiac and respiratory outcomes, it specifically reports PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization associations which are directly relevant to the review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma-related ED visits which are respiratory emergency department visits, (4) time-series study design with Poisson regression, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 and other pollutants. Although the study found no significant positive associations for PM2.5, it still analyzed PM2.5 and reported effect estimates, making it eligible for inclusion in a systematic review.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure (along with its components) and respiratory hospitalizations in children. The study uses a time-series design (daily counts with Poisson regression), reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 4.1% excess risk, 95% CI 1.8-6.4 for PM2.5), and meets all inclusion criteria. While the study also examines PM2.5 components, PM2.5 itself is analyzed as a primary exposure.

The study examines cardiovascular outcomes (AMI, CHF, ischemic stroke) rather than respiratory hospitalizations. Although the study meets other criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, case-crossover design, reports effect estimates with CIs), the outcome does not match the inclusion criteria which specifically requires respiratory hospitalization or ED visits.

The study examines coarse particulate matter (PM2.5-10), which refers to particles between 2.5 and 10 micrometers in diameter, not PM2.5 (fine particulate matter ≤2.5 µm). This does not meet the inclusion criterion requiring PM2.5 exposure. While the outcome (respiratory hospitalizations) and study design (case-crossover) are appropriate, and effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported, the exposure is explicitly coarse particles, not PM2.5.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is respiratory emergency department visits for asthma, (4) case-crossover study design, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (RR IQR=1.03, 95% CI 1.02-1.04 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Although the study examines multiple exposures including ozone and pollen, PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory emergency department visits, (4) case-crossover design as stated in title and methods, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals for respiratory outcomes (asthma/wheeze, COPD, bronchitis), and (6) published in English.

While this is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design examining respiratory ED visits with effect estimates, the primary exposure is ozone (O3), not PM2.5. Although the abstract mentions fine particulate matter was included in copollutant models, PM2.5 is not the main exposure of interest and no separate PM2.5 effect estimates are reported. The study does not meet inclusion criterion #2.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations using appropriate time-series methodology (GAM and DLNM) and reports quantitative effect estimates, the primary outcome is hospitalization COSTS rather than hospitalization occurrence or counts. The study does not report relative risk or odds ratios for respiratory hospitalization events themselves, but rather percentage changes in costs. This does not meet the inclusion criteria which specifically requires respiratory hospitalization or ED visits as the outcome.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (COPD admissions). It uses a time-series design with Poisson regression, reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (RR=1.25, 95% CI=1.22-1.27 for spring; RR=1.24, 95% CI=1.23-1.26 for winter), and meets all inclusion criteria. COPD is a respiratory condition and hospital admissions for COPD qualify as respiratory hospitalizations.

While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design), it does not report a relative risk, odds ratio, or equivalent effect measure with confidence interval. The study only reports correlation coefficients (R values) and regression coefficients from a linear model, not the standardized effect estimates (RR/OR) required for systematic review inclusion.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure, (3) respiratory hospitalizations are reported as one of the outcomes, (4) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are provided (1.14% increase per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5 for respiratory admissions), and (5) the abstract is in English. The study examines multiple outcomes including respiratory hospitalizations, which is directly relevant to the systematic review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 (fine particulate matter <2.5 microns), (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (pneumonia and asthma), (4) study design is time-series, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals for multiple lag periods, and (6) appears to be published in English (or translated). The study uses appropriate statistical methods (generalized additive model with Poisson regression) and provides quantitative effect estimates.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure includes PM2.5 and its components, (3) outcome is respiratory emergency department visits for pneumonia, (4) case-crossover study design (time-stratified), (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs (e.g., 18.2% increase, 95% CI 8.8-28.4% for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Pneumonia is a respiratory condition and ED visits are an appropriate outcome for this review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study comparing two analytical approaches, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as an exposure with specific effect estimates reported, (3) the outcome is respiratory disease hospitalizations, (4) both time-series and case-crossover designs are used, (5) quantitative effect estimates are reported as percentage increases with confidence intervals for each 10 μg/m3 increment in PM2.5, and (6) the abstract is in English. The study provides specific numerical results for PM2.5 effects on respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) the outcome is asthma hospital admissions (a respiratory hospitalization), (4) both time-series and case-crossover designs are used, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported (e.g., 30.2% increase with 95% CI: 13.4-49.6% for PM2.5), and (6) the article is in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically included and analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (pneumonia), (4) time-series design explicitly stated, (5) while the abstract doesn't provide the exact RR/OR with CI, it reports quantitative associations and effect estimates (256 fewer admissions per 10 µg/m3 decrease), suggesting effect measures were calculated. The only uncertainty is whether the full paper reports RR/OR with confidence intervals, but the use of Poisson regression in a time-series study strongly suggests this information is available in the full text.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and COPD hospitalizations using a time-series design (GAM with Poisson distribution and DLNM). The study reports quantitative effect estimates (percent increases) with 95% confidence intervals for the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations. COPD admissions are a respiratory hospitalization outcome. All inclusion criteria are met.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other PM fractions) and respiratory hospital admissions. The study uses Poisson regression models and reports statistically significant associations, which implies quantitative effect estimates are provided. PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, and respiratory-cause hospital admissions is one of the outcomes. Meets all inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly measured as exposure, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (asthma readmissions), (4) case-crossover design is specified, (5) reports OR with 95% CI (OR=1.082, 95% CI=1.008-1.162), and (6) published in English. Asthma readmissions are a respiratory hospitalization outcome.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original case-crossover epidemiological study, (2) examines PM2.5 exposure (along with PM10), (3) outcome is asthma-related hospital visits which are respiratory hospitalizations, (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI (e.g., 1.26, 95% CI 1.22-1.30), and (6) published in English. The study analyzes both PM10 and PM2.5, with PM2.5 being one of the exposures examined.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as one of the exposures, (3) the outcome is respiratory (asthma) emergency department visits, (4) both time-series and case-crossover designs are used, (5) quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported (RR and OR with 95% CI), and (6) it is published in English. Although PM2.5 was not significantly associated with the outcome, the study still examined PM2.5 and reported effect estimates for it, which is valuable for a systematic review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 and respiratory outcomes, (2) exposure is source-specific PM2.5, (3) outcomes include asthma and COPD hospitalizations and ED visits, (4) uses a modified time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports excess rates (ERs) with specific quantitative estimates (e.g., 0.5%-3.1%, 1.3%-1.7%, 2.1%-3.4%), and (6) published in English. The study analyzes PM2.5 from multiple sources, which is acceptable per inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (asthma admissions), (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports OR with 95% CI for PM2.5 (OR 1.09; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.13), and (6) published in English. Asthma hospitalizations are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) uses time-series design with Poisson regression/GAM, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates as percent increases with specific values for different lag periods, and (6) published in English. All exclusion criteria are avoided.

Although this study examines PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) exposure and uses a time-series design with effect estimates, the outcome is acute otitis media (AOM) hospitalizations, not respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits. AOM is an ear infection, not a respiratory condition, and therefore does not meet the inclusion criteria for respiratory outcomes.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using distributed lag nonlinear models; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure; (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (pneumonia, COPD, asthma); (4) the study design is time-series based on daily admissions and daily air pollutant data; (5) quantitative effect estimates are reported (RR with 95% CI for PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations); (6) the abstract is in English.

This is an original case-crossover study examining the association between air pollution (including PM2.5 as one component of the AQHI) and respiratory ED visits for asthma. The study reports odds ratios with 95% CIs. Although the primary exposure is the composite AQHI index, PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) is explicitly stated as one of the three pollutants included in the index. The outcome is respiratory ED visits, the design is case-crossover, and quantitative effect estimates are provided.

While this study examines respiratory ED visits and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the primary exposure is thunderstorms and power outages, not PM2.5. PM2.5 is only examined as a mediating/modifying factor of the thunderstorm-health relationship, not as the main exposure of interest. The study does not provide direct PM2.5 exposure-respiratory hospitalization associations that would be relevant for a systematic review on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure, (3) respiratory hospitalizations are the primary outcome, (4) it uses a time-series design, (5) quantitative effect estimates are reported (0.9-4.5% increase per 10 units PM2.5 increase), and (6) it is published in English. The abstract clearly describes a multi-city time-series analysis examining PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations with specific effect estimates provided.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and adult pneumonia hospital visits including ED visits. The abstract indicates effect estimates were calculated (mentions statistically significant impacts and effect estimates), though specific numerical values are not provided in the abstract. Pneumonia hospitalizations are respiratory hospitalizations. Meets all inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (ICD-9: 460-519), (4) time-series study design explicitly stated, (5) reports RR with 95% CI for respiratory causes (RR=1.049, 95% CI 1.019-1.078), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it includes respiratory hospitalizations as a separate outcome of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design with Poisson regression; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) respiratory hospitalizations are among the outcomes studied; (4) the study design is time-series; (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported for respiratory hospitalizations (e.g., 23.5% increase for PM2.5-10, 12.8% for PM10); (6) the article is in English. Although PM2.5 itself showed significant association primarily with circulatory diseases, the study analyzes PM2.5 and its chemical constituents in relation to respiratory hospitalizations, making it relevant for the systematic review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using ecological time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalization among other outcomes, (4) study design is explicitly time-series, (5) the abstract indicates associations were estimated with effect measures (mentions 'risk' and 'associations'), and (6) appears to be published in English. While the study examines multiple outcomes (mortality and hospitalizations for various causes), respiratory hospitalization is specifically mentioned as one of the outcomes analyzed.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations. It reports relative risks (RRs) with appropriate statistical modeling. While it also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly includes respiratory admissions as an outcome. The study meets all inclusion criteria: original epidemiological research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and reports RR estimates.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma-related ED visits which are respiratory ED visits, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although the abstract primarily reports results for other pollutants (O3, CO, NO2), PM2.5 is clearly stated as one of the exposures examined in the study.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory disease hospitalizations. It uses a distributed lag nonlinear model (DLNM), which is a time-series approach. The study reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations. All inclusion criteria are met.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure (from various sources), reports respiratory emergency department visits as the outcome, and provides odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. The study is clearly published in English and reports quantitative effect estimates.

This is an original ecological time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations in children. The study uses Poisson regression GAM with appropriate lag structure and reports quantitative effect estimates (89 additional hospitalizations per 5µg/m3 increment in PM2.5). While the abstract does not explicitly state RR/OR with confidence intervals, it reports quantitative associations between PM2.5 increments and hospitalization increases, which can be converted to effect estimates. The study meets all major inclusion criteria: original epidemiological research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and quantitative effect measures.

This is an original time-series epidemiological study that examines PM2.5 (among other exposures) and emergency hospital admissions for respiratory diseases. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals. Although the primary focus is on coarse PM (PMc), the methods clearly state that PM2.5 was analyzed as part of the exposure assessment and controlled for in models, making PM2.5 one of multiple exposures analyzed. This meets inclusion criteria per the exception 'unless PM2.5 is one of multiple exposures analyzed.'

This is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design to examine the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations in New York State. The study reports hazard ratios (HRs) as effect measures. While the primary focus is on evaluating geo-imputation methodology, it still presents quantitative effect estimates for the PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization association, meeting all inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using Poisson time-series regression, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospital admissions, (4) study design is time-series, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CIs for respiratory hospitalizations, and (6) published in English. While the study also examines mortality and cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly analyzes hospital admissions due to respiratory causes as one of its outcomes.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) respiratory ED visits (specifically asthma) are among the outcomes examined, (4) the study design is case-crossover, (5) quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported (OR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.03-1.23 for PM2.5 and asthma), and (6) the article appears to be published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes and other pollutants, this does not disqualify it from inclusion as PM2.5 and respiratory ED visits are clearly analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5 (wildfire-sourced), (3) outcome includes respiratory ED visits, (4) time-series design explicitly stated, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI (0.47% increase per 1 μg/m3 for respiratory diseases with CI: 0.30%, 0.64%), and (6) published in English. While the PM2.5 is specifically from wildfire sources, it is still PM2.5 exposure which meets the inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations (asthma admissions) as the outcome, and provides quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (12% increase with 95% CI = 6-18% on warm days; 3% increase with 95% CI = 0-8% on cool days).

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as an exposure, (3) respiratory hospitalizations are included as outcomes (lower respiratory tract infections and COPD), (4) case-crossover design is specified, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (e.g., 2.8% increase for lower respiratory tract infections, 1.6% for COPD), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines cardiac outcomes and other particle sizes, it clearly reports PM2.5 effects on respiratory hospitalizations with effect estimates.

This is an original time-series study examining the association between short-term PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (as well as circulatory). The study reports quantitative effect estimates with credible intervals for both respiratory and circulatory outcomes. It meets all inclusion criteria: original epidemiological research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and reports effect estimates with confidence/credible intervals.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using two-stage time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures, (3) Outcome is hospital admissions for AECOPD (acute exacerbation of COPD), which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) Study design is time-series as stated in methods, (5) Reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (RR=1.093, 95% CI 1.06-1.13 for PM2.5), and (6) Published in English. The study analyzes multiple pollutants but PM2.5 is specifically included with quantitative effect estimates.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations (influenza hospital visits, ICD-10 J11). The study uses appropriate statistical methods (GLM with quasi-Poisson) that would generate effect estimates. While the abstract doesn't explicitly state RR/OR values, the methods and results sections indicate quantitative associations were assessed. Influenza hospital visits qualify as respiratory hospitalizations. The focus on interactive effects with viral exposure is a specific research question but doesn't disqualify the study from examining the PM2.5-hospitalization association.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original ecological time series study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations, and reports relative risk estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 6% increase with 95%CI: 1.4-10.8 for children; 6.8% increase with 95%CI: 0.5-13.5 for elderly).

This study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure (among other pollutants), includes respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits as outcomes (COPD mentioned specifically), uses what appears to be a time-series design based on Poisson regression for short-term impacts, and reports rate ratios with statistical significance. While the study examines multiple chronic diseases (not only respiratory), it does include COPD which is a respiratory condition with hospitalization outcomes. The study design appears to be time-series given the focus on short-term impacts and daily variations in air quality.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures, (3) respiratory hospitalization is reported as an outcome, (4) quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are provided (0.33%-1.1% increase in odds for all-age and non-senior respiratory hospitalization per 7.6 μgm-3 increase in PM2.5), and (5) it is published in English. Although it is a multi-pollutant study, PM2.5 results are specifically reported for respiratory hospitalization.

This is an original time-series study using Poisson regression with DLNM to examine the association between PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations (AECOPD). The study reports quantitative effect estimates including relative cumulative risks and percentage increases in hospitalizations per 10 μg/m3 increase in pollutants. COPD exacerbations are a respiratory hospitalization outcome. All inclusion criteria are met.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and includes respiratory outcomes (ARDS, pneumonia) among hospitalized patients with quantitative effect estimates, it fails to meet the study design criterion. This is a cohort study examining chronic air pollution exposure and COVID-19 morbidities among hospitalized patients, not a time-series or case-crossover design. The study uses hospitalization records and assigns chronic exposure based on residential ZIP code, then follows patients for outcomes, which is characteristic of a cohort design rather than the required time-series or case-crossover approaches.

This study meets the inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome includes respiratory hospital admissions (ICD-10: J00-J99), (4) Poisson generalized linear models were used which would provide effect estimates, and (5) it appears to be a peer-reviewed publication in English. While the abstract does not explicitly state effect estimates with confidence intervals, the methodology described (Poisson GLM in a time-series framework) would generate such estimates. The study analyzes multiple pollutants including PM2.5, which is acceptable per inclusion criteria.

This study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and pneumonia hospitalizations (a respiratory outcome). However, the abstract does not explicitly report quantitative effect estimates (RR, OR, or equivalent with confidence intervals), only stating that associations were statistically significant (P<0.05) and describing relative rankings of pollutant effects. The study appears to be published in Chinese, though the abstract is provided in both English and Chinese. Without access to the full text to confirm whether quantitative effect estimates are reported and the publication language, the decision remains uncertain.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using generalized additive models; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly listed as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) Outcome is COPD hospital admissions, which is a respiratory hospitalization; (4) Study design is time-series based on the methodology described (GAM with lag effects, controlling for temporal trends); (5) Reports percentage change in hospital admissions per 10 µg/m³ increase, which is a quantitative effect estimate; (6) Published in English. COPD hospitalizations are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization that fits the outcome criteria.

While this is an original case-crossover study examining respiratory ED visits with quantitative effect estimates, the exposure is PM10 and PM2.5-10 (coarse particles between 2.5-10 µm), not PM2.5 (fine particles ≤2.5 µm). The study explicitly states it assessed PM10 and PM2.5-10 contained in Saharan dust, and does not report PM2.5 exposure or effects. This does not meet the inclusion criterion requiring PM2.5 exposure.

While this is an original case-crossover study that includes PM2.5 exposure and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the outcome is clinically-defined COPD exacerbations experienced in patients' homes, not respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits. The abstract explicitly states these exacerbations were detected early in home settings as part of disease management, distinguishing them from ED visits and hospital admissions.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma hospital admissions (respiratory hospitalization), (4) time-series design explicitly stated, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI for PM2.5 (3% increase per 1 μg/m3, 95% CI 1.006% to 1.052%), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported.

While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, respiratory hospitalization outcome, appropriate study designs, effect estimates with CIs), the primary exposure of interest is coarse particulate matter (PM10-2.5), not PM2.5. The abstract explicitly states 'We did not find significant effects of fine particulate matter (PM2.5)' on asthma hospitalizations. Although PM2.5 was analyzed, it was not the main exposure and showed null findings, making this study inappropriate for a systematic review specifically focused on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using generalized additive models; (2) PM2.5 exposure is explicitly measured and analyzed; (3) Outcome is emergency department visits for respiratory condition (COPD exacerbations); (4) Study design is time-series (ecological study with lag analysis and seasonal patterns); (5) Reports quantitative effect estimates (5.8% increase in visits per 10 µg/m³ PM2.5 with attributable fraction); (6) Published in English with Spanish translation. The study design described as 'ecological' with generalized additive models, lag structures, and adjustment for temporal confounders is consistent with time-series methodology.

While this study examines PM2.5 among other pollutants and reports respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome with effect estimates (RRs), it is described as a 'spatio-temporal ecological study' rather than a time-series or case-crossover design. The study design appears to be an ecological study examining geographical units over time, which does not meet the specific study design inclusion criteria requiring time-series or case-crossover methodology.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure is wildfire-specific PM2.5, (3) outcome includes both respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits, (4) case-crossover study design, (5) reports OR with 95% CI (OR=1.014, 95% CI=1.012-1.016), and (6) published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it separately reports results for respiratory diseases which are relevant to the review.

The study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, examines PM2.5 exposure, and reports respiratory hospitalizations and ER visits as outcomes. However, the abstract does not explicitly state whether quantitative effect estimates (RR, OR, or equivalent with confidence intervals) are reported - it only mentions 'statistically significant association (p < 0.05)'. Without confirmation that specific effect estimates with confidence intervals are provided in the full text, the study cannot be definitively included per criterion 5.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory ED visits. It reports quantitative effect estimates (IRR). Although the outcome is upper respiratory tract infections specifically (rather than all respiratory conditions), URTI is a respiratory condition leading to ED visits, which meets the outcome criteria. PM2.5 was analyzed as one of multiple exposures with effect estimates reported.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory emergency department visits in Atlanta from 1993-2004. The study uses Poisson generalized linear models and reports associations (effect estimates) between pollutants and respiratory ED visits. It meets all inclusion criteria: original epidemiological study, includes PM2.5 exposure, respiratory ED visit outcome, time-series design, and reports quantitative effect estimates with positive associations mentioned for multiple pollutants.

This is an original time-series study that includes PM2.5 as an exposure variable and respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome. The study reports relative and attributable risks calculated using generalized linear models. While the study examines multiple pollutants and outcomes, it specifically mentions NO2 associations with respiratory disease admissions and NO2 with asthma-related admissions, and PM2.5 is listed as one of the exposures analyzed. The study meets all inclusion criteria despite being a multi-exposure, multi-outcome study.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and asthma hospitalizations using time-series analysis with Poisson regression, the results explicitly state that 'no significant associations were found for PM2.5...with asthma-related...hospitalizations.' This suggests no quantitative effect estimate (RR, OR, or equivalent with confidence interval) for the PM2.5-asthma hospitalization association was reported. The study appears to be primarily focused on surveillance capacity building and describing disparities rather than reporting specific effect estimates for PM2.5 and respiratory outcomes.

While this is an original time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits with quantitative effect estimates, the primary exposure is PM10, not PM2.5. Although the abstract mentions that PM10 is 'mostly PM2.5', the actual exposure measured and analyzed is PM10, and the effect estimates reported are for PM10 (per 100 µg/m3 increase in PM10). The study does not report separate PM2.5 measurements or PM2.5-specific effect estimates, which is required for inclusion.

While this study meets several inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, time-series design, quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals), the outcome is doctors' house calls for respiratory diseases rather than respiratory hospitalizations or emergency department visits. The study explicitly distinguishes house calls from hospital admissions, making it incompatible with the specified outcome criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using generalized additive models; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) Outcome is respiratory hospital admissions; (4) Time-series design analyzing daily hospital admissions and air pollution concentrations; (5) Reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (0.885% increase per 10μg/m3 PM2.5, 95%CI: 0.414%-1.358%); (6) Published in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported.

Although this is an original case-crossover study examining PM2.5 exposure with quantitative effect estimates, the outcome is respiratory mortality, not respiratory hospitalization or emergency department visits as required by the inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalization (asthma hospital admissions), (4) it uses a time-series study design with DLNM, (5) it reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for multiple pollutants including PM2.5, and (6) the article is published in English. Although the abstract primarily highlights NO2 results, it clearly states that PM2.5 was analyzed and found to have effects on childhood asthma admissions.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using GAM time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as an exposure among multiple pollutants, (3) AECOPD hospitalization is a respiratory outcome, (4) time-series design using generalized additive model, (5) reports relative risk (RR) estimates, and (6) published in English. While the study also examines stroke and MI, it includes respiratory hospitalizations (AECOPD) which is relevant to the review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design (Poisson regression with daily hospital admissions), examines PM2.5 as one of the exposures, reports respiratory hospitalizations (asthma admissions) as the outcome, and provides quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (RR=1.04, 95% CI=1.02-1.07 for PM2.5).

This is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design (Poisson generalized additive model) examining the association between PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (AECOPD admissions). The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5. COPD exacerbations are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization. The study appears to be published in English (or translated). All inclusion criteria are met.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations using a generalized additive model (consistent with time-series design). The study reports quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals (e.g., 0.2% increase with 95% CI: 0.1-0.7% for PM2.5). It meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series analytical approach, and reports RR/effect estimates with CIs.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure includes PM2.5 (along with PM10), (3) outcome includes respiratory ED visits (asthma, COPD, respiratory conditions), (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although the exposure is defined as smoke events based on both PM10 and PM2.5, PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposure metrics used.

This is a longitudinal birth cohort study, not a time-series or case-crossover design. The exposure is assigned based on postal code at birth and children are followed longitudinally for 13 years, which does not meet the required study design criteria. While it examines PM2.5 components, reports effect estimates with CIs, and includes respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits as outcomes, the cohort design is incompatible with the systematic review's inclusion criteria.

While this is an original case-crossover study examining respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits with quantitative effect estimates, the primary exposure is ozone, not PM2.5. Although PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) is mentioned as a co-pollutant that was adjusted for, the study's focus and all reported effect estimates are for ozone exposure. The inclusion criteria require PM2.5 as the primary exposure of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly measured and analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (asthma and bronchiolitis), (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (OR: 1.22, 95% CI=1.03-1.44 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines other exposures (SO2, wind direction), PM2.5 is specifically analyzed with quantitative effect estimates.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and includes respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome using Poisson regression (time-series design), it appears to be a health impact assessment that estimates attributable cases rather than reporting relative risks or odds ratios with confidence intervals. The 95% CI reported (204-749 million RMB) refers to economic losses, not epidemiological effect estimates. The study reports absolute numbers of cases attributed to pollution rather than quantitative effect measures (RR/OR) per unit increase in PM2.5.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis to examine the association between PM2.5 (among other particulate matter measures) and respiratory hospitalizations among elderly adults. The study reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals. Although the main finding indicates no significant association between PM2.5 and respiratory admissions, PM2.5 was explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, making it relevant for the systematic review.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure (from wildfire smoke) and emergency department visits for respiratory outcomes including asthma exacerbation and unspecified respiratory disorder. The study uses time-series methodology with distributed lag models and reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals. It meets all inclusion criteria.

The study meets several inclusion criteria: it uses time-series analysis, examines PM2.5 exposure, and assesses respiratory hospitalizations. However, the abstract describes this as an intervention study evaluating the effect of a heating technology substitution program rather than a traditional epidemiological study examining the direct association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations. The abstract does not clearly indicate whether quantitative effect estimates (RR, OR, or CI) for the PM2.5-hospitalization relationship are reported. The study appears to evaluate a policy intervention's impact on both PM2.5 levels AND hospitalizations, which may be an interrupted time series design rather than a standard time-series analysis of PM2.5-health associations. Full text review would be needed to determine if it reports the required effect estimates for PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization association.

While this is a time-series study that includes PM2.5 as an exposure and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals for respiratory hospital admissions, the primary exposure is the composite Air Quality Health Index (AQHI) rather than PM2.5 specifically. The study focuses on validating the AQHI as a combined measure of multiple pollutants. The effect estimates reported are for AQHI, not for PM2.5 alone. Additionally, the primary outcome appears to be mortality, with hospital admissions used for validation purposes.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original case-crossover epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly measured as an exposure, (3) respiratory hospitalizations are examined as outcomes (including COPD, pneumonia, and asthma), (4) uses case-crossover design with conditional logistic regression, (5) reports associations/effect estimates for respiratory outcomes, and (6) published in English. While the abstract does not explicitly state confidence intervals, the use of conditional logistic regression in a case-crossover study and mention of 'significant associations' strongly suggests quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals were calculated.
The outcome is atrial fibrillation (AF) hospitalization, which is a cardiovascular outcome, not a respiratory hospitalization or ED visit. This does not meet inclusion criterion #3.

The study examines myocardial infarction (MI) hospitalizations as the outcome, not respiratory hospitalizations. Additionally, the exposure is PM10 (particulate matter <10 µm), not PM2.5 (particulate matter ≤2.5 µm). Both the exposure and outcome do not meet the inclusion criteria.

While this is a time-series study that includes PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations as outcomes, the primary exposure of interest is temperature, not PM2.5. The study examines how air pollutants (including PM2.5) modify temperature-hospitalization associations rather than directly assessing the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations. The effect estimates reported are for temperature effects modified by pollution, not for PM2.5 effects on respiratory outcomes.

This is an original time-series study examining the association between PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and emergency department visits for pediatric asthma exacerbations. The study reports rate ratios with statistical measures. While the primary focus is on comparing different exposure metrics rather than establishing the PM2.5-health association itself, it meets all inclusion criteria: original epidemiological study, includes PM2.5 exposure, respiratory ED visits as outcome, time-series design, and reports quantitative effect estimates (rate ratios).

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original ecological time-series study, (2) exposure includes fine particulate matter (PM2.5), (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (asthma, COPD), (4) uses time-series design with appropriate statistical methods, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with percent increases for 10 µg/m3 increase in PM2.5, and (6) appears to be published in English (abstract is in English). While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes and other pollutants, it specifically reports PM2.5 effects on respiratory hospitalizations.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and mentions respiratory outcomes (asthma, chronic bronchitis) and hospitalization, it appears to be primarily a health economic evaluation study focused on calculating economic losses rather than reporting epidemiological effect estimates (RR, OR) for the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations. The study reports economic losses in yuan and number of cases, but does not appear to report relative risks or odds ratios with confidence intervals for the PM2.5-hospitalization association, which is required for inclusion.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes hospitalizations and ED visits for asthma/wheeze (respiratory conditions), (4) case-crossover study design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., OR: 1.08, 95% CI: 1.01, 1.15), and (6) published in English. Asthma and wheeze are respiratory conditions and the outcomes explicitly include hospitalizations and ED visits.

This study meets the key inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is respiratory hospital admission, (4) the study design is time-series as stated. While the abstract does not explicitly mention effect estimates with confidence intervals, it reports significant associations and appears to be a quantitative analysis that would typically report such measures. The study analyzes multiple pollutants including PM2.5, which is acceptable per inclusion criteria.

This is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design to examine the association between PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and emergency department visits for pediatric asthma. The study reports quantitative effect estimates (RR: 1.10, 95% CI: 1.05, 1.16) for PM2.5 exposure. Although the primary focus is on demonstrating a methodological approach (regression trees) and examining multipollutant mixtures, it meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 as one of the exposures, respiratory ED visits as outcome, case-crossover design, and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma emergency department visits which is a respiratory ED visit, (4) time-series design is clearly stated, (5) quantitative effect estimates are reported (4% increase in asthma ED visits associated with PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants were studied, PM2.5 was specifically analyzed and reported.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (influenza and pneumonia) using a time-series design (GAM/DLNM) and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the outcome measure is hospitalization COSTS rather than hospitalization incidence or counts. The study quantifies the economic burden (percentage change in costs) rather than the health outcome (risk of hospitalization). This does not meet the inclusion criteria which specifically requires respiratory hospitalization or ED visit as the outcome, not the economic costs associated with those hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) outcome is ED visits for pneumonia which is a respiratory condition, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (14.0% increase, 95% CI 5.1-23.8% for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Pneumonia is a respiratory condition requiring emergency department visits, which qualifies as the outcome of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) outcome is bronchiolitis hospitalization (a respiratory hospitalization), (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover method, and (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (26-41% increased risk for premature infants). The study examines bronchiolitis, which is a respiratory condition requiring hospitalization, making it appropriate for a review on respiratory hospitalizations.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations among other outcomes. The study uses daily ZIP code counts with Poisson regression, which is characteristic of a time-series design. Quantitative effect estimates are reported (percent increases with specific values for respiratory admissions). The study meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and reports effect estimates.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure (along with O3) and respiratory hospitalizations in Beijing using conditional Poisson regression (a time-series approach). The study reports quantitative effect estimates including relative excess risk due to interaction with 95% CI (1.65%, 95%CI: 0.46%-2.84%). Although the study examines both PM2.5 and O3, PM2.5 is explicitly one of the exposures analyzed, meeting inclusion criteria. The outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, the design is time-series, and effect estimates are provided.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure (in Los Angeles County) and respiratory hospitalizations for COPD. The study uses generalized additive models to analyze daily hospital admissions, which is appropriate for time-series analysis. Although PM2.5 was only measured in one of three counties, the abstract indicates effect estimates were calculated (coefficients mentioned). COPD admissions qualify as respiratory hospitalizations. The study appears to report quantitative effect estimates even though specific RR/OR values are not provided in the abstract.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory emergency department visits as the outcome, and provides quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (0.84%; 95% CI: 0.33-1.35% per 10-μg/m3 increase in PM2.5).

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization, (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although PM2.5 showed no significant effects while coarse PM was the primary finding, PM2.5 was analyzed and effect estimates are reported, making it eligible for inclusion in a systematic review on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome includes respiratory emergency department visits, (4) time-series study design, (5) reports statistically significant percentage increases (effect estimates) for respiratory ED visits, and (6) published in English. While the study also examines other pollutants and circulatory outcomes, PM2.5 and respiratory ED visits are specifically analyzed and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure includes PM2.5 (along with PM2.5-bound metallic elements), (3) outcome is asthma emergency department visits which qualifies as respiratory ED visits, (4) case-crossover study design is specified, (5) reports statistically significant risk estimates with conditional logistic regression models, and (6) published in English. The study explicitly reports quantitative associations between PM2.5 and asthma ED visits.

This study meets the key inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospital visits, (2) uses a time-series design with Poisson regression, (3) examines hospital visits for acute respiratory infections and pneumonia, and (4) reports associations between PM2.5 and respiratory outcomes with statistical modeling. While the abstract does not explicitly state effect estimates with confidence intervals, the use of Poisson regression models and reporting of 'significant correlations' and 'notable associations' strongly suggests quantitative effect estimates are reported in the full text. The study examines PM2.5 among other metrics (oxidative potential, black carbon), which is acceptable per inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure (among other pollutants), reports respiratory hospitalizations as the outcome, and provides quantitative effect estimates (ORs with 95% CIs). The study explicitly reports OR=1.0179 (95% CI 1.0097-1.0260) for PM2.5 and respiratory/pneumonia hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) outcome is asthma-related emergency hospital admissions which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) time-series approach is clearly stated, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 (RR 1.01, 95% CI 1.0003-1.03 for 5 µg/m3 increase), and (6) published in English. Although the outcome is specific to asthma rather than all respiratory conditions, asthma hospitalizations are a subset of respiratory hospitalizations and are commonly included in such reviews.

This is a simulation study, not an original epidemiological study with real health outcome data. The respiratory ED visits were simulated using Monte Carlo methods rather than observed from actual patient data. While it uses time-series methodology and includes PM2.5 as one of the exposures, it does not meet the inclusion criterion of being an original epidemiological study that reports actual associations between PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations.

While this is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure, the outcome is medication purchase/sales rather than respiratory hospitalization or emergency department visits. The study does not meet inclusion criterion 3, which specifically requires respiratory hospitalization or ED visit as the outcome.

While this is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations for asthma, the abstract explicitly states that 'calculating relative risk inappropriate' and the results section only reports significant associations for NO2, not PM2.5. No quantitative effect estimate (RR, OR, or CI) for PM2.5 is reported in the abstract, which is a critical inclusion requirement.

The study examines cardiovascular hospitalizations, not respiratory hospitalizations. Although PM2.5 exposure is assessed and the study uses a case-crossover design with effect estimates, the outcome does not meet the inclusion criteria which specifically requires respiratory hospitalization or ED visits.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using DLNM; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization; (4) time-series design with daily data and lag analysis; (5) reports relative risk estimates with specific quantitative values for PM2.5 (0.23% increase in hospitalization risk per 10% increase in PM2.5 at 5-day lag); (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 results are clearly reported.

This is an original time-series epidemiological study examining the association between PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory ED visits. The study reports associations between fine particulate matter and cardiovascular outcomes, and between respiratory ED visits and ozone. It uses Poisson models to estimate health associations, which would provide effect estimates with confidence intervals. The study meets all inclusion criteria: original research, includes PM2.5 exposure, includes respiratory ED visits as an outcome, uses time-series design, and appears to report quantitative effect estimates.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (COVID-19), the study design is a retrospective cohort study using patient-level data from hospital records, not a time-series or case-crossover design as required by the inclusion criteria. The study analyzes individual patient outcomes (mortality, ICU admission) in relation to environmental exposures at postcode level, which is characteristic of a cohort design rather than the required ecological time-series or within-person case-crossover approach.

The outcome is acute kidney injury (AKI) emergency department visits, not respiratory hospitalization or ED visits. Although the study meets other criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, case-crossover design, reports OR with CI), it does not meet the respiratory outcome requirement.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using quasi-Poisson regression with DLNM, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures, (3) respiratory-related emergency hospital admissions are reported as an outcome, (4) time-series study design, (5) reports risk associations with quantitative effect estimates, and (6) published in English. The abstract indicates positive associations were found between PM2.5 and respiratory-related emergency admissions with effect measures reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using GAM with Poisson regression, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as one of the exposures, (3) outcome is emergency room visits for respiratory diseases, (4) time-series design indicated by GAM controlling for temporal trends and day-of-week effects, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs for PM2.5 (1.4% increase per 10 μg/m³ in urban, 1.5% in suburban areas), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is emergency department visits for asthma (a respiratory condition), (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although the abstract primarily reports results for O3, NO2, and PM10, PM2.5 is clearly stated as one of the pollutants examined.

Although this study meets criteria for exposure (PM2.5), study design (case-crossover), and has effect estimates with confidence intervals, the outcome is emergency department visits for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), which is a neurodegenerative disease, not a respiratory hospitalization or ED visit. The systematic review specifically requires respiratory outcomes, not neurological conditions.

This is an original epidemiological study using an interrupted time-series design to examine the association between PM2.5 exposure (from wildfire smoke) and pediatric respiratory emergency department and urgent care visits. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (excess respiratory visits per day). It meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory ED/urgent care visits as outcome, time-series design, and reports effect estimates with CIs.

This is a long-term cohort/ecological study examining 12-year follow-up effects, not a time-series or case-crossover design. The study design involves exposure data from 1999-2000 and outcome data from 2012, which is characteristic of a cohort study examining long-term effects rather than short-term associations. The inclusion criteria specifically require time-series or case-crossover designs.

While this is a time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations with effect estimates, the primary exposure of interest is aeroallergens (tree pollen, fungi, weeds), not PM2.5. PM2.5 is used as a stratifying variable to examine effect modification rather than as the main exposure. The study does not report direct effect estimates for PM2.5 on respiratory hospitalizations, which is the focus of the systematic review.

While this is a case-crossover study examining PM2.5 exposure with effect estimates reported, the primary outcome is mental health emergency department visits, not respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits. Although respiratory mortality is mentioned in the results, it is a secondary outcome and no specific effect estimate for respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits is provided.

While this study examines PM2.5 as one of multiple exposures and reports respiratory ED visits as an outcome, the primary exposure of interest is influenza, not PM2.5. The study uses time-series models to estimate influenza-attributable respiratory ED visits, then uses spatial models to examine correlates (including PM2.5) of this influenza burden. PM2.5 is treated as a covariate/correlate rather than the primary exposure. The study design does not directly assess the association between PM2.5 and respiratory ED visits in the manner required for inclusion.

This is an original epidemiological study using time-series design (Poisson regression on daily counts) that examines PM2.5 among other pollutants. The study reports respiratory hospitalizations as one of the outcomes with quantitative effect estimates and 95% CIs. Although the primary focus is on ultrafine particles, PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed and reported with effect estimates for respiratory hospital admissions.

This is an original time-series epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (and its components) in relation to respiratory ED visits (asthma and COPD). The study reports statistically significant associations, which implies quantitative effect estimates were calculated. Although the abstract does not explicitly state RR/OR values with confidence intervals, it describes statistical modeling approaches and reports significant positive associations for respiratory outcomes. PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposures analyzed during the superstation period.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and respiratory (asthma) hospitalizations, it does not use a time-series or case-crossover design as required. The study uses Poisson and linear regression models examining the association between monthly average pollutant concentrations and hospitalization costs/length of stay, which is a different analytical approach. Additionally, the primary outcomes are healthcare costs and length of stay rather than hospitalization incidence or risk. The study does not report RR or OR for respiratory hospitalization risk.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly measured as one of multiple air pollutants, (3) outcome is respiratory ED visits for asthma/wheeze, (4) uses Poisson time-series design, (5) reports rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although the abstract primarily highlights ozone results, PM2.5 and its components are clearly analyzed as exposures.

This is an original time-series epidemiological study that examines PM2.5 (among other pollutants) as an exposure and respiratory ED visits as an outcome. The study uses generalized additive models on time-series data from 1992-1996. The abstract explicitly mentions PM2.5 in single-pollutant models showing positive effects on respiratory diagnosis groups, and reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals. Although the final multipollutant model emphasizes O3 and SO2, PM2.5 results are reported in single-pollutant models, meeting the inclusion criteria.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure using a time-series design with effect estimates, the primary outcome is 'critical illness' admissions broadly (including cardiovascular, neurological, and respiratory disorders), not specifically respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits. Although respiratory diseases are analyzed as a subgroup, the study does not report separate effect estimates for respiratory outcomes specifically, which is required for inclusion in a systematic review focused on respiratory hospitalizations.

This is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design to examine PM2.5 exposure and ED visits. While the study reports no significant association for overall respiratory outcomes, it does examine respiratory outcomes (upper respiratory infections, asthma, COPD) and provides quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals. The study meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory ED visits as one of the outcomes examined, case-crossover design, reports RR with 95% CI, and appears to be in English.

This is an original epidemiological study examining the association between PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) and asthma emergency department visits in children. The study uses a time-series design (Poisson regression with daily ED counts regressed against air pollution). It reports a quantitative effect estimate (relative rate of 1.15 with 95% CI 1.08-1.23 for an 11 µg/m3 change in fine PM). Asthma ED visits are a respiratory outcome. The study meets all inclusion criteria.

This is an original time-series study that includes PM2.5 as one of the exposures (measured 1992-1994), examines respiratory hospitalizations (pneumonia and COPD admissions in elderly patients) as outcomes, uses Poisson regression to estimate effects, and reports quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals. While the abstract primarily reports mortality results and PM10/TSP findings, it explicitly states that hospital admissions for respiratory conditions (pneumonia, COPD) were analyzed for the 1992-1994 period when PM2.5 was measured. The study meets all inclusion criteria.

While this is an original case-crossover study examining PM2.5 exposure with effect estimates reported, the outcome is ambulance emergency calls (AECs) rather than respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits. Although the study mentions respiratory diseases-related AECs in the conclusions, the primary outcome is ambulance calls, which precede and are distinct from actual hospitalizations or ED visits. The study does not specifically report effect estimates for respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits.

The study includes PM2.5 exposure, respiratory ED visits (asthma), and appears to use time-series methods. However, the primary focus is on characterizing pollutant interactions and multi-collinearity rather than reporting health effect estimates. The asthma ED visit analysis is described as 'an example' provided at the end. It's unclear whether quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported for PM2.5 and respiratory outcomes, or if this is primarily a methodological paper about pollutant correlations. The abstract suggests the health analysis may be secondary/illustrative rather than the main objective.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 exposure clearly specified with thresholds, (3) respiratory ED visits as outcome, (4) case-crossover study design, (5) reports odds ratios from conditional logistic regression, and (6) published in English. The abstract mentions 'increased odds' suggesting quantitative effect estimates are reported.

While this is an original time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits with a quantitative effect estimate (RR=1.23, 95% CI 1.07-1.41), the primary exposure is PM2.5 zinc concentration (a component of PM2.5), not PM2.5 mass concentration itself. The study focuses specifically on the metal composition (zinc) rather than total PM2.5 exposure, which does not meet the inclusion criteria requiring PM2.5 as the exposure of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations as the outcome, and provides multiple odds ratios with confidence intervals (e.g., 1.87(1.17-2.97) for asthma, 2.18(1.20-3.97) for LRTI). The study is published in English and reports quantitative effect estimates.

This study meets several inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design (Poisson GAM), examines PM2.5 as one of multiple exposures, includes respiratory ED visits as one of the outcomes, and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals. However, the abstract only presents results for SO2 associations with neurologic and circulatory outcomes, not for PM2.5 or respiratory outcomes. The study likely contains PM2.5-respiratory ED visit associations in the full text since both were measured, but this cannot be confirmed from the abstract alone. The decision is uncertain because the relevant data may exist but are not presented in the abstract.

This is an original case-crossover study that examines both ozone and PM2.5 exposure in relation to asthma-related ED visits. While the primary focus appears to be on ozone (based on the title and the reported effect estimate for ozone), PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposures analyzed. The study meets the inclusion criteria: it uses a case-crossover design, examines respiratory ED visits (asthma-related), includes PM2.5 as an exposure, and reports quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals. Although only the ozone effect estimate is provided in the abstract, the study analyzed PM2.5 and likely reports those results in the full text.

The outcome is venous thromboembolism (VTE), not respiratory hospitalization or ED visit. VTE is a cardiovascular/hematological condition, not a respiratory condition. This fails the outcome inclusion criterion.
